description: We're Echoa, a data and analytics team.
summary: AQUACITIES 3D is an interactive 3D web dashboard that helps residents, responders, and businesses in Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, see flood and fire risk at street and address scale. Users explore a dark 3D city map, raise a flood-level slider to watch real road classes inundate in order of vulnerability, click a point or search a CEP or street address for a flood-risk score, and toggle a wildfire visualization with flame and smoke overlays. A GeoMarketing module scores commercial viability by combining hydrologic risk with simple urban indicators. Live weather and 7-day rainfall come from the Open-Meteo API and feed a transparent risk formula based on precipitation, surface impermeability, elevation, and distance to local water bodies. An optional Databricks layer can store assessments and event history. The project matters because mid-sized Brazilian cities face seasonal floods and urban or vegetation fires, yet local decisions are often made without an intuitive, place-based view of risk
details:
AQUACITIES 3D is a full-stack web dashboard created by team ECHOA (Guilherme Leone and Arthur Argeri Zilio) for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge. It is a place-based decision-support tool for farms and agricultural producers around Ribeirão Preto, in the sugarcane belt of São Paulo, Brazil, where heavy rain, waterlogging, dry-season heat, and vegetation fires affect field operations, soil health, water use, and harvest risk.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

A producer can search a CEP or address, or click a point on a 3D map, to evaluate conditions at a specific farm or field.

- NASA Farm Panel: uses the NASA POWER daily agroclimatology API (community AG) to read 30 days of rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), temperature (T2M, T2M_MAX), humidity (RH2M), root-zone and surface soil wetness (GWETROOT, GWETTOP) and solar radiation. These feed a transparent Farm Climate Risk indicator that separates drought stress from waterlogging. Example for Ribeirão Preto (Oct 13 to Nov 11, 2026): 95.6 mm rain, 25.2 °C mean temperature, root-zone wetness 0.52, Farm Climate Risk LOW.

- Real fire detections: NASA FIRMS VIIRS and MODIS active-fire data are shown on the map (13 detections near Ribeirão Preto in the last 7 days), so producers can see burning near fields, mills, and the urban edge.

- Flood Map 3D: a MapLibre 3D map shows how rising water affects real road classes in order of vulnerability. A flood-risk score combines precipitation, surface impermeability, estimated elevation, and distance to local water bodies (Córrego Ribeirão Preto, Represa Municipal, Córrego Retiro Saudoso, Rio Pardo), helping highlight low-lying, poorly drained ground.

- GeoMarketing: a location-viability view that weighs hydrologic risk for farm warehouses, mills, and agribusiness sites at the rural-urban fringe.

Live weather from Open-Meteo complements the NASA data. All external calls fail gracefully with fallbacks.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Intended users are sugarcane and mixed-crop producers, agronomists, cooperatives, and municipal teams supporting rural areas. The tool gives one visual place to see how rainfall, soil moisture, heat, and fire combine at a chosen farm, supporting decisions that protect fields, conserve water, reduce losses from waterlogging or fire, and help farms adapt management and rotation choices as climate shifts. The architecture can be extended to other agricultural regions in Brazil.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Software-only web application. Frontend: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Axios, Turf.js. Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, NumPy, Pydantic. Data: NASA POWER, NASA FIRMS, Open-Meteo, CARTO/OpenMapTiles, ViaCEP, OpenStreetMap Nominatim. Optional Databricks for storing assessments.

CREATIVITY

We combined a city-scale 3D situation room with a farm climate-risk view, so flood, waterlogging, drought, and fire are read together on one map. The Farm Climate Risk indicator translates NASA agro-climate and satellite fire observations into simple decision language producers can act on.
